security_spec.violation_condition: Linux kernel context-switches a RISC-V hart with active CTR (Smctr/Ssctr) state without saving and restoring the CTR buffer (ctrsource, ctrtarget, ctrdata across all depth entries), cycle counter (CC/CCV), and CTR configuration, allowing the next scheduled task to read the previous task's control flow transfer history.
security_spec.summary: Smctr/Ssctr CTR buffer holds branch history (source/target PCs, transfer type, cycle count) accessible via indirect CSRs (Smcsrind/Sscsrind); failing to save/restore this state on context switch leaks precise inter-process control flow data that defeats KASLR and enables side-channel key extraction.

findings.finding: The switch_to() macro saves/restores FPU state (via __switch_to_fpu), vector state (via __switch_to_vector), and envcfg (via __switch_to_envcfg), but has zero CTR (Smctr/Ssctr) state save/restore. On hardware implementing Smctr/Ssctr without Smstateen (where mstateen0.CTR would not gate access), or where firmware has set mstateen0.CTR=1, CTR buffer entries (ctrsource, ctrtarget, ctrdata across all depth entries), sctrstatus (WRPTR, FROZEN), sctrctl, sctrdepth, and the cycle counter (CC/CCV) are not preserved across context switches, allowing a subsequent task to read the previous task's control flow transfer history.
findings.snippet:
#define switch_to(prev, next, last)        \
do {                                        \
    struct task_struct *__prev = (prev);     \
    struct task_struct *__next = (next);     \
    __set_prev_cpu(__prev->thread);          \
    if (has_fpu())                           \
        __switch_to_fpu(__prev, __next);     \
    if (has_vector() || has_xtheadvector())  \
        __switch_to_vector(__prev, __next);  \
    if (switch_to_should_flush_icache(__next))\
        local_flush_icache_all();            \
    __switch_to_envcfg(__next);              \
    ((last) = __switch_to(__prev, __next));  \
} while (0)

spec_citations.excerpt: The CTR buffer entries are logically accessed via the indirect register access mechanism defined by the Sscsrind extension. The siselect index range 0x200 through 0x2FF is reserved for CTR logical entries 0 through 255. When siselect holds a value in this range, sireg provides access to ctrsource, sireg2 provides access to ctrtarget, and sireg3 provides access to ctrdata.

When mstateen0.CTR=0 and the privilege mode is less privileged than M-mode, the following operations raise an illegal-instruction exception: Attempts to access sctrctl, vsctrctl, sctrdepth, or sctrstatus; Attempts to access sireg* when siselect is in 0x200..0x2FF; Execution of the SCTRCLR instruction.
When mstateen0.CTR=0, qualified control transfers executed in privilege modes less privileged than M-mode will continue to implicitly update entry registers and sctrstatus.

On reset, all writable mstateen bits are initialized by the hardware to zeros. [...] Software at each privilege level should set its respective stateen CSRs to indicate the state it is prepared to allow less-privileged software to access. For OSes and hypervisors, this usually means the state that the OS or hypervisor is prepared to swap on a context switch, or to manage in some other way.

Implementations that support Smctr/Ssctr but not Smstateen/Ssstateen may observe reduced performance. Because Smctr/Ssctr introduces a significant number of new CSRs, it is desirable to avoid save/restore of CTR state when possible. [...] Without Smstateen/Ssstateen, a hypervisor is required to save/restore guest CTR state on every context switch.
The CtrCycleCounter is reset on writes to __x__ctrctl, and on execution of SCTRCLR, to ensure that any accumulated cycle counts do not persist across a context switch.

findings.finding: No CTR (Smctr/Ssctr) ISA extension detection, no sctrclr instruction emulation, no sctrstatus/sctrctl/sctrdepth CSR definitions, no CTR buffer save/restore fields in thread_struct, and no signal frame CTR state preservation. The kernel has zero knowledge of the CTR extension.
findings.snippet: (no CTR-related code exists in this file)

findings.finding: No TSK_CTR_* or similar asm-offsets defined for CTR state. Without these offsets, low-level assembly context-switch code (__switch_to in entry.S) cannot save/restore CTR state even if it wanted to.
findings.snippet: (no CTR-related offsets exist in this file)

findings.finding: The SMSTATEEN0 bit definitions cover HSENVCFG (bit 62), AIA (bits 58-60), and SSTATEEN0 (bit 63), but do not include the CTR bit (bit 54 in mstateen0/hstateen0, per Smstateen spec). Without this bit definition, the kernel cannot discover or enable CTR access for S-mode, and KVM cannot delegate CTR to guests.
findings.snippet:
/* Smstateen bits */
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC_SHIFT  58
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC        (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_SHIFT        59
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA              (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_AIA_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL_SHIFT   60
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL         (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_HSENVCFG_SHIFT   62
#define SMSTATEEN0_HSENVCFG         (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_HSENVCFG_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_SSTATEEN0_SHIFT  63
#define SMSTATEEN0_SSTATEEN0        (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_SSTATEEN0_SHIFT)

spec_citations.excerpt: Machine State Enable 0 Register (mstateen0) bit layout: ...{bits: 1, name: 'CTR'}... The CTR bit (bit 54) controls access to CTR register state from privilege modes less privileged than M-mode.
Hypervisor State Enable 0 Register (hstateen0) bit layout: ...{bits: 1, name: 'CTR'}... The hstateen0.CTR bit controls access to supervisor CTR state when V=1.

findings.finding: KVM vCPU config initialization sets hstateen0 bits for HSENVCFG, AIA, and SSTATEEN0, but does not set the CTR bit (bit 54). This means VS-mode guests can never access CTR state even if the hardware implements Smctr/Ssctr, because hstateen0.CTR remains 0.

spec_citations.excerpt: If the H extension is implemented and mstateen0.CTR=1, the hstateen0.CTR bit controls access to supervisor CTR state when V=1. [...] When mstateen0.CTR=1 and hstateen0.CTR=0, both VS-mode accesses to supervisor CTR state and VS-mode execution of SCTRCLR raise a virtual-instruction exception.

findings.finding: KVM VCPU load saves/restores guest CSRs (VSSTATUS, VSIE, etc.) and FPU/vector context, but performs no save/restore of CTR state (sctrctl (vsctrctl), sctrstatus, sctrdepth, or CTR buffer entries via sireg*/siselect range 0x200-0x2FF). A VM using CTR (if hstateen0.CTR were set) would leak its CTR history to the next VM or host task.

spec_citations.excerpt: Because Smctr/Ssctr introduces a significant number of new CSRs, it is desirable to avoid save/restore of CTR state when possible. A hypervisor is likely to leverage State Enable to trap on the initial guest access to CTR state, delegating CTR and enabling save/restore of guest CTR state only once the guest has begun to use it.

findings.finding: No RISCV_ISA_EXT_SMCTR or RISCV_ISA_EXT_SSCTR entry in the ISA extension data array. The kernel cannot detect whether the hardware supports CTR, so it cannot conditionalize CTR save/restore or even warn about missing CTR support.
findings.snippet: (no SMCTR/SSCTR ISA extension data entry exists; smstateen is the only related entry at line 581)

spec_citations.excerpt: The machine-level extension, Smctr, encompasses all newly added Control Status Registers (CSRs), instructions, and behavior modifications for a hart across all privilege levels.

The corresponding supervisor-level extension, Ssctr, is essentially identical to Smctr, except that it excludes machine-level CSRs and behaviors not intended to be directly accessible at the supervisor level.
